title: Spot the difference: Hubble spies another globular cluster, but with a secret
caption: The globular cluster Messier 53, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 5024 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 60000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Thousands upon thousands of brilliant stars make up Messier 53, the globular cluster in this Hubble image. Bound tightly by gravity, it is roughly spherical and grows denser toward its heart.

Such clusters are far from rare, and more than 150 exist in the Milky Way. Messier 53 lies on the outer edges of our galaxy, roughly as far from the galactic center as it is from the Sun. William Herschel, not known for poetic flourishes, once counted a globular cluster among the most beautiful sights he could recall in the heavens.

Messier 53 holds an unusually large number of blue stragglers. Because all of a globular cluster's stars are expected to form at about the same time, they should follow a trend set by the cluster's age and their masses. Blue stragglers break that rule, looking brighter and younger than they should. Their exact nature is still a mystery, but they most likely arise when stars in the packed center pass very close to each other or even collide.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.44 x 3.54 arcminutes) and distance (60000 light years), the frame spans roughly 60 × 62 light-years. Its light set out about 60,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and infrared exposures from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The infrared exposure records light the eye cannot see, and Hubble's sharp view separates thousands of individual stars.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Messier 53, also cataloged as NGC 5024, lies about 60,000 light-years away in Coma Berenices. Since globulars are far older and bigger than open clusters, astronomers expect them to contain fewer massive blue stars and more old red ones. The picture combines visible and infrared exposures from the Advanced Camera for Surveys' Wide Field Channel and spans about 3.4 arcminutes.
alt: A roughly spherical cluster of thousands of brilliant stars, growing denser toward its center.
